findings.claim: Examiners reward answers that consider these tensions rather than simply listing the four aims.
findings.truth: Invented claim about what examiners reward. No published statement of this kind exists; the point can be made as study advice without attributing it to examiners.
findings.evidence: house rule: no fabricated examiner claims / invented mark-scheme wording

findings.claim: scholars such as Maimonides observed that a court executing even one person in seventy years was considered severe
findings.truth: The saying is Mishnah Makkot 1:10, where Rabbi Eliezer ben Azariah says a Sanhedrin that executes even once in seventy years is destructive. Maimonides did not originate it; he later codified the strict rules of evidence in the Mishneh Torah.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, Capital punishment in Judaism (Mishnah Makkot 1:10; Rabbi Eliezer ben Azariah)

findings.claim: The Lord's Prayer (Matthew 6) makes forgiveness conditional on the willingness to forgive others: “Forgive us our sins, as we forgive those who sin against us.”
findings.truth: That wording is the modern liturgical Lord's Prayer, not the Gospel text. Matthew 6:12 (NIV) reads 'forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors'. The conditional teaching the spec names is Matthew 6:14-15.
findings.evidence: spec Theme 3, Christian perspective: forgiveness sources are Matthew 18:21-22 and Matthew 6:14-15; NIV Matthew 6:12

findings.claim: Whole lesson teaches pacifism, war and conscientious objection as part of this theme, with two practice questions set on it ('Give two religious reasons why a person might refuse to fight in a war', 'Explain two contrasting religious views on pacifism').
findings.truth: Pacifism, war and conscientious objection appear nowhere in this specification: 'pacifis', 'conscientious', 'Quaker' and standalone 'war' return zero matches. Theme 3 covers crime and punishment, forgiveness, and good/evil/suffering only; there is no war-and-peace theme in this route. This is AQA/Edexcel territory. OPTIONS: (a) rebuild the lesson around forgiveness (Matthew 18:21-22, Matthew 6:14-15, Micah 7:18, Qur'an 42:30 and 64:14, Guru Granth Sahib 866, metta and Angulimala) plus the spec's 'examples of forgiveness arising from personal beliefs' (Gee Walker, Desmond Tutu, Martin Luther King), demoting pacifism to a clearly labelled enrichment box; (b) keep the lesson but replace the two pacifism practice questions with forgiveness questions and add a line saying pacifism is background, not assessed content. RECOMMEND (a): the two practice questions cannot be set on this paper, so a student who revises them loses time.
findings.evidence: spec, Theme 3 tables for all six traditions (Crime and Punishment / Forgiveness / Good, Evil and Suffering); zero spec matches for pacifism, war or conscientious objection
findings.ruling: Leave: scope/question re-setting is a build item (relabel queue).

findings.claim: Note: this lesson uses Pali terms as the spec specifies Pali primary.
findings.truth: Authoring scaffolding left in student-facing prose. It also misstates the spec, which cites the Pali Canon and Dhammapada but says nothing about a 'Pali primary' rule. Delete the sentence.

findings.claim: Examiners look for this kind of critical engagement rather than a simple list of different views.
findings.truth: Invented claim about examiner behaviour. Say it as study advice instead.

findings.claim: The extended evaluation question awards marks for both, plus a spelling, punctuation and grammar (SPaG) weighting.
findings.truth: The 15-mark evaluation question is assessed on AO2 only. The spec's objectives grid gives this paper AO1 25% and AO2 25% of the qualification, so its 120 marks split 60 AO1 and 60 AO2. Each of the four themes carries 30 marks: the 2, 5 and 8-mark parts are the 15 AO1 marks and the evaluation question is the 15 AO2 marks.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1 assessment objectives and weightings grid (Route A: AO1 25%, AO2 25% on this paper); spec summary of assessment (2 hours, 50%, 120 marks plus 6 SPaG, four compulsory themes)

findings.claim: Examiners have identified these recurring problems in students' evaluation answers.
findings.truth: Invented examiner claim. The advice that follows is sound; only the attribution is fabricated.

findings.claim: examiners require you to engage seriously with at least one opposing view. A one-sided response is capped at the lower bands regardless of content quality.
findings.truth: The requirement is real but it comes from the question rubric, not from examiners: the evaluation question tells candidates to consider more than one point of view. The effect is that a one-sided answer cannot reach the top band, not that it is capped at 'the lower bands'.
findings.evidence: spec Component overview: compulsory questions focusing on knowledge, understanding and evaluation; AO2 is analysis and evaluation of more than one view

findings.claim: Every lesson sets two 8-mark questions, one of them labelled 'Explain Two Contrasting Views' ('Explain two contrasting religious views on capital punishment / on pacifism / on the cause of suffering / on whether it is always right to forgive').
findings.truth: The 8 marks are right for this paper, but the stem is another board's wording: the 'two contrasting beliefs' stem belongs to AQA, where it is worth 4 marks. On this paper the 8-mark part asks candidates to explain teachings from two different religious traditions and to refer to a source of wisdom or authority. OPTIONS: (a) relabel the second 8-mark question in each lesson to the two-traditions stem, keeping the content; (b) delete it, since each theme carries only one 8-mark part. RECOMMEND (a): the contrast material is useful and the two-traditions stem covers it.
findings.evidence: spec summary of assessment (120 marks over four themes, 30 marks each) with the objectives grid giving 15 AO1 and 15 AO2 marks per theme, i.e. one 2, one 5, one 8 and one 15-mark part
findings.ruling: Leave: scope/question re-setting is a build item (relabel queue).

findings.claim: The 2, 5 and 8-mark practice questions test exam technique, not religion: 'Give two things an evaluator must do to gain top marks', 'Describe the three-level approach to using sources of authority', 'Explain two common mistakes students make in evaluation answers'.
findings.truth: These carry real mark tariffs but could never be set: every question on this paper is on the four themes' religious content. OPTIONS: (a) keep the exam-skills teaching but swap the three questions for Good and Evil content questions at the same tariffs; (b) keep them and relabel them as practice drills rather than exam questions. RECOMMEND (a): a tariff on the question tells the student it is exam-shaped.
findings.evidence: spec summary of assessment: compulsory questions focusing on knowledge, understanding and evaluation of the identified themes
findings.ruling: Leave: scope/question re-setting is a build item (relabel queue).

findings.claim: Every 15-mark mark scheme ends '[15 marks + SPaG 5%]'.
findings.truth: SPaG is 6 marks on this paper. The 5% figure is the qualification-level weighting of SPaG across AO1 and AO2 (12 marks in total across the two papers that carry it), not a bonus on one question.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1: 'The total weighting for spelling, punctuation and grammar will be 5% of the sum of all marks available for assessment objectives AO1 to AO2 i.e. 12 marks overall'; summary of assessment: 120 marks plus 6 for SPaG

findings.claim: Flashcards 1 and 3 ask the identical question about retribution; flashcards 2 and 4 ask the identical question about reformation. Each pair gives a different answer.
findings.truth: Duplicate question text with two different answers. Not wrong, but the student sees the same card twice and cannot tell which answer is wanted. Worth a de-dup pass, not a fact edit.

findings.claim: The Guru Granth Sahib (GGS 866) teaches that the truly brave person is one who accepts hardship without complaint and does not pick quarrels.
findings.truth: The reference matches the spec's named Sikh forgiveness source, so the citation is safe, but the paraphrase could not be verified against a text of Ang 866 within this session's fetch budget. Check the paraphrase against a translation before the next narration pass.

findings.claim: The Talmud (Berakhot 9:5) contains a passage in which the rabbis discuss the obligations to bless God for both good and evil
findings.truth: Berakhot 9:5 is a Mishnah, not a Talmud passage, though the Mishnah sits inside the Talmud so the label is loose rather than false. The spec cites it simply as 'Berakhot 9:5'.
findings.evidence: spec Theme 3, Jewish perspective: 'Berakhot 9:5, Avodah Zarah 3b, Deuteronomy 30:15-19'

findings.claim: Eva Clarke, who survived the Holocaust as a child
findings.truth: Eva Clarke was born in Mauthausen concentration camp on 29 April 1945, days before liberation, so she survived as a newborn rather than as a child. Not mark-affecting; correct it if the paragraph is edited for any other reason.
findings.evidence: Eva Clarke's published biography (born in Mauthausen, April 1945; lives in Cambridge)

findings.claim: Philosophical and religious explanations for evil: theodicy, Original Sin, karma and the Three Poisons.
findings.truth: 103 characters, over the 100-character description limit the validator enforces. Length is not a fact error, so no edit is written here; trim it if the lesson is rewritten (for example 'Why evil and suffering exist: theodicy, Original Sin, karma and the Three Poisons.').
findings.evidence: character count

summary: Four lessons checked. Scripture, doctrine and answer keys are almost all sound; the damage is concentrated in fabricated examiner and mark-scheme claims (7 instances, 11 edits) and one wrong attribution (the seventy-years Sanhedrin saying given to Maimonides instead of Mishnah Makkot 1:10). Three scope questions need Tom's ruling: lesson 2 teaches pacifism and conscientious objection, which appear nowhere in this specification; every lesson sets a second 8-mark question in another board's 'contrasting beliefs' form; lesson 4 sets tariffed practice questions on exam technique that could never appear on the paper.
